h1: Topping up with water to hit your target gravity
title: Topping Up to Hit Your Target Gravity | Craft Beer School
desc: How to top up homebrew wort with water to bring a high gravity down to target, with the simple dilution sum, safe water and when to add it.
teaser: Overshot your gravity? A few litres of the right water fixes it. Here is the one-line sum and how to add it safely.
standfirst: Hitting a gravity higher than planned is a nice problem. Diluting with water brings it back to target, gives you more beer and costs almost nothing. It needs the right sum and clean water. Here is how we do it.
sections: Gravity points times volume stays the same

Dilution rests on one fact: adding water changes the volume but not the total amount of sugar. Brewers express that sugar as gravity points multiplied by litres. A wort at 1.060 has 60 points. Twenty litres of it holds 60 times 20, or 1,200 point-litres.

To find the volume you need at a lower target, divide the total by the target points. Every dilution and concentration calculation on brew day comes back to this sum. Once you have it, you can do it on a phone calculator with sticky hands.

The same sum works in reverse. If you want to know what gravity you will get after adding a known amount of water, divide the point-litres by the new volume. Twenty litres at 1.060 topped up to 22 litres gives 1,200 divided by 22, about 55 points, or 1.055.

Say you collected 18 litres at 1.060, but the recipe called for 1.054.

  • Total sugar: 60 points times 18 litres is 1,080 point-litres.
  • Volume at target: 1,080 divided by 54 is 20 litres.
  • Water to add: 20 minus 18 is 2 litres.

Add 2 litres, stir well and take a new reading. It should land close to 1.054. If it reads slightly high, the wort probably was not mixed. Water is lighter than wort and sits on top until stirred.

Wort going into a fermenter must stay sanitary. The top-up water needs to be as clean as the wort. Good options:

  • Water boiled for a few minutes and cooled in a covered, sanitised pot.
  • Sealed packaged drinking water from a fresh bottle or can.
  • Reverse osmosis water from a clean home unit, collected into a sanitised container.

Avoid untreated municipal water straight from the tap. Chlorine and chloramine react with malt compounds to form chlorophenols, which taste of plasters or medicine at very low levels. A Campden tablet removes both. One tablet is enough for a large volume of water, so a fraction of one easily covers a top-up.

Borewell water brings a different problem. It can be high in minerals or carry bacteria, depending on the source. Unless you know it is clean and soft, boil it or use packaged water for any top-up that goes straight into the fermenter.
Add it before the boil if you can

The best moment to correct gravity is before the boil. Take a pre-boil reading. If it is high, add water to the kettle then. The boil sanitises it, the hops see the final volume and the bitterness works out as planned.

Post-boil top-ups are still fine but carry two side effects. First, they dilute bitterness. Hops were added to a smaller, stronger wort. Diluting by 10% lowers IBU by roughly 10%. Second, they dilute colour slightly. Both are small for a top-up of a litre or two. Our guide to original and final gravity explains the readings.
Topping up as a method, not a fix

Extract brewers and small-kettle brewers often top up on purpose. They boil a concentrated wort of 10 to 12 litres in a stockpot, then dilute it to 20 litres in the fermenter. In hot Indian weather this has a useful side effect. Several litres of chilled water added to boiled wort brings the temperature down much faster than any chiller.

The trade-off is hop utilisation. A strong wort extracts bitterness less efficiently than a weak one, so partial boil brewers usually need more bittering hops. Recipe software can correct for this if you enter your boil volume honestly.

Do not top up a beer that is already fermenting to correct gravity. Adding water after fermentation starts dilutes alcohol and flavour. Fresh water also carries oxygen into beer that should not see it. Correct gravity before pitching or not at all.

Also check the volume. If your fermenter only holds 23 litres with headspace, adding 4 litres to an already full batch can leave no room for krausen. In that case you might accept the higher gravity and enjoy a slightly stronger beer, provided the yeast can handle it. Knowing which way to go comes from understanding how gravity, bitterness and yeast interact.
Write the sum in your log

Copy the formula into the front of your brew log: volume needed equals points times litres divided by target points. Next brew day, take a pre-boil reading and run the sum before the burner goes on. If you need water, add it then.
faqs: How do I calculate how much water to add to lower gravity?
Multiply current gravity points by current litres, divide by target gravity points to get the new volume, then subtract the current volume.
Can I top up with tap water?
Only if it is boiled or treated to remove chlorine and chloramine. Untreated tap water can cause medicinal off-flavours.
Yes, roughly in proportion. Adding 10% more volume lowers IBU by about 10%.
